# The many faces of Karma

No important name has only one face. **Karma** appears ​as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and a digital temple. This post looks at each face in ‌turn: the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the symbols and sanctuaries, and the afterlife that brought the canonical spelling into the present.

## At a ‌Glance

- **Restored name:** Karma
- **ASCII form:** karma
- **Meaning:** "Deed, action"
- **Domain of influence:** Action, Consequence
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** कर्म (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Karma** (*karma*) — Deed, ​Action, the Law of Consequence · Deed, action — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Action, Consequence". The name means "Deed, action".

**Karma** ​is the law that no deed evaporates: every act plants its seed, and the harvest is the life — and lives — that follow. From a plain Vedic noun ​for “ritual action” it grew into the doctrine that drives Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike: the moral physics by which the universe keeps its books without a bookkeeper.

​PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Karma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/karma/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The ​plain ASCII form *karma* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

‌The name is attested in Devanagari as **कर्म**. Etymologically it means "Deed, action".

The canonical spelling **Karma** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *karma* contains the ​same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **कर्म**.

The ​scholarly transliteration is *Karma*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Karma is written in Devanagari as कर्म
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin ‌equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈkɑːrmə/** — Sanskrit ​(IAST: Karma).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Kar-** — From √kṛ, “to do, make”; the r is syllabic-flavoured, the a long “ah”.
- **-ma** — The abstract noun: “action”, “deed” — ‌and by extension, the law that deeds breed consequences.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “KAHR-muh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Pali** — Kamma
- **the** ​— law of moral causation across all Indian traditions

The word begins as a plain noun — “deed” — and becomes the engine of the universe. The neuter gender ​marks the noun as a principle, not a person.

## Mythology

Karma has no biography because it outranks every biography: it is the rule all biographies obey. Its ‘mythology’ is ​the doctrine’s own history — from the Vedic ritual’s power to bind, through the Upaniṣads’ interiorization, to the great vehicles’ global export — and the countless stories, from Nala ​to Savitri, in which its arithmetic drives the plot.

### From Ritual to Moral Physics (Upaniṣadic Revolution)

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad relocates karma: no longer the ritual act alone but the ​intention behind every act — ‘one becomes good by good action, evil by evil action’. The ritual economy of the Brahmins became the moral economy of the universe, and ‌no priest was needed to run it.

### The Owner of the Deed (Buddhist Formulation)

The Buddha’s formula is the doctrine’s cleanest statement: beings are the owners of their deeds, ​the heirs of their deeds — nowhere else does the inheritance come from. Karma in Buddhism is intention (cetanā) itself; the deed’s fruit follows like the wheel follows the ‌ox.

### The Story Where It Breaks (Savitri Cycle)

The Mahābhārata’s Savitrī tale stages the doctrine’s limit-case: Satyavān’s life exhausted by karma’s count, Yama arrives on schedule — and the ​wife’s flawless speech wins the husband back. The epic never denies the law; it shows a love so exact in its dharma that the law’s own keeper must honour ‌it.

### The Subtle Dust (Jain Mechanics)

Jainism made karma physical: a subtle matter that clings to the soul like dust to a wet cloth, weighing it into rebirth. The ​doctrine’s imagery — the soul’s lightness restored by austerity until it rises like a flame released — is the most materialist eschatology India produced.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography ‌associated with Karma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Seed and the Fruit** — Every deed is a seed; ​the fruit may ripen in this life or a later one — but it ripens.
- **Action by Mind, Word, Deed** — Karma accrues by thought, speech, and body — ‌the three doors of action the law watches.
- **The Burning Off** — Karma can be exhausted by experience — burned like a field of stubble — or bound by ​attachment like a new seed.
- **Liberation Beyond It** — Mokṣa, nirvāṇa: the states beyond karma’s reach — the doctrines’ common horizon.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Karma ​survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Karma ‌leaves no temple — it is the reason temples leave merit. The stūpas’ circumambulation-paths, the ghāṭs’ staircases into the rivers, and the endless charity-inscriptions of Indian epigraphy are its ‌monuments: every recorded gift is a seed on record.

## Realm & Domain

**Karma** is the law that no deed evaporates: every act plants its seed, and the harvest is ‌the life — and lives — that follow. From a plain Vedic noun for “ritual action” it grew into the doctrine that drives Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike: ​the moral physics by which the universe keeps its books without a bookkeeper.

### The Seed and the Fruit

Every deed is a seed; the fruit may ripen in this ​life or a later one — but it ripens.

### Action by Mind, Word, Deed

Karma accrues by thought, speech, and body — the three doors of action the law ‌watches.

### The Burning Off

Karma can be exhausted by experience — burned like a field of stubble — or bound by attachment like a new seed.

### Liberation Beyond It

​Mokṣa, nirvāṇa: the states beyond karma’s reach — the doctrines’ common horizon.

## Across Cultures

Karma is the one doctrine shared by Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain without alteration of name ​— the subcontinent’s common physics. The West received it through theosophy and thence into the global vernacular, where ‘karma’ now means cosmic payback in any language; classical comparisons run ‌to the Egyptian heart-weighing and the Greek Adrasteia.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

The ​word entered every major language as a loan — among the few Sanskrit terms to do so. It underwrites the theory of rebirth, the ethics of non-harm (the deed’s ​victim returns as one’s debtor), and the quietist strand of Indian political thought: the revolution you cannot make today, your karma will make eventually.
